summary:
South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between adults is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017 following what Amnesty International described as a 2017 "gay witch hunt" in which 32 personnel were criminally charged. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition exists and the surgery requirement is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court (Yeongdong) ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court, sitting en banc, ruled that transgender people with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are unmarried, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that had uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

Facilities access is a live source of harm. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled, finally and without appeal, that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research presented by the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong on 20 March 2024 found that trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; one 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding in urination and leaving school early.

In healthcare, the state human rights watchdog NHRCK has flagged a "transgender blind spot in hospitalisation": the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. In November 2024 the Constitutional Court recognised same-sex partners' healthcare rights. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. Violence at LGBTQ events is documented: at an Incheon Pride event about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants and organisers filed charges against pastors while accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride roughly 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters.
tangentialFactors:
Transgender people encounter the state most visibly through the military. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, a transgender conscript, was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

The 2017 military investigation into gay personnel operated by using dating-app contacts to identify soldiers; Amnesty International characterised it as a witch hunt and criticised it publicly. Personnel were charged over consensual conduct, with at least one six-month prison sentence.

Discrimination burden is documented across the life course. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published in Epidemiology and Health on 27 June 2025 mapped milestones and stigmatisation for 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, recording pervasive discrimination at school, in work and in transition-related care. A 2014 study found 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths harassed by classmates; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults had faced harsh discrimination in the preceding year. Among outed LGBTQ people, 16.1% were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma.

Contact tracing during the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster outed LGBTQ people; doxing and online harassment rose, and one transgender man told NBC News he felt threatened simply walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report characterises South Korea's overall record as relatively positive, with free media and active civil society, but documents persistent discrimination against LGBT people. LGBT organisations can in principle register: an NGO won a registration case at Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, with the government appealing to the Seoul High Court and the Supreme Court, and HRW has criticised years of bureaucratic obstruction of such registrations. A commercial gay travel guide (July 2026) rates Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods broadly positive for visitors while stressing the military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition and absence of a national anti-discrimination law.
localsOnly:
Restroom access shapes daily life for trans residents. School-age trans students avoid school facilities, with documented cases of holding in urination and leaving school early rather than risk being outed. Adult trans people have received police advice to avoid public restrooms, and a court has since held that such advice infringed personal rights.

Hospitalisation remains poorly served: the national health ministry declined to draft guidelines for transgender patients, leaving trans people to negotiate admission, ward placement and handling of gendered records with individual hospitals on a case-by-case basis.

Legal gender recognition is achievable without surgery following the May 2024 ruling, and trans parents of minor children can be recognised provided they are unmarried. Marriage to a partner of the same sex is unavailable, as is joint adoption by same-sex couples, so partners have no automatic hospital-visitation, inheritance or parental standing beyond what individual rulings or contracts supply.

Trans residents bear documented harassment in education and employment, high rates of classmate harassment among LGBTQ youth, and a significant share of outed people being pushed toward conversion therapy. Openly LGBTQ people face exposure through public health contact tracing and subsequent online harassment.
outOfScopeNotes:
How transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system is unresolved on this record: no source describes a birth-sex versus identity placement rule, a special unit, or any solitary or segregation practice. The most prominent state-placement litigation on file concerns the military discharge of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su rather than civilian incarceration.

A Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry (25 January 2023) covering a Supreme Court decision on a transgender person with minor children changing gender in the family relations register could not be retrieved (HTTP 403). The underlying fact is corroborated by encyclopedic coverage dated 24 November 2022; the 2023 framing and any procedural detail from that entry remain unverified.

Claims about current visitor experience in Seoul's LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods rest on a single commercial travel guide and have not been corroborated by an independent monitoring source.
